newsitem.title: UK: Dollar steadies, eyes German jobless data for cue.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steadies, eyes German jobless data for cue.

text.p: The dollar steadied below the 12-week high it set against the yen overnight after comments by a Japanese official reinforced expectations that interest rates there are not about to rise from record lows anytime soon.

The focus switched to dollar/mark early in the European session before the release of the July German jobless report. Data that shows the economy is too fragile to allow the Bundesbank to raise interest rates significantly in the mark's defence will undermine the German currency, analysts said.
"Dollar/yen was bid overnight but all eyes are on Germany now," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.

The dollar was at 1.8795/00 marks at 0745 GMT from 1.8788 late Tuesday in Europe. It was at 119.00/10 yen, little changed from 119.01/11 late yesterday but down from the 119.58 high it hit overnight. That was the highest it had been since May 13.

Talk the Bundesbank could engineer higher money-market rates by switching to variable-rate tenders has intensified in recent weeks as the mark has slumped to five-year lows in trade-weighted terms, falling particularly sharply against the dollar.
Expectations that the German central bank has limited scope to raise rates against the backdrop of fragile growth has encouraged traders to bet against the mark.

Dollar bulls will get further encouragement if today's German jobless report comes in much weaker than expected. Economists polled by Reuters expect the number of jobless in Germany rose by a seasonally adjusted 15,000 in July after the 11,000 increase reported in June.

Meantime, the dollar was supported against the yen after Japanese Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura said overnight that the low interest rate policy that the Bank of Japan was following still had positive economic effects.
He added that control of Japan's key rate, the official discount rate, was solely in the hands of the Bank of Japan.

Still, his comments reinforced expectations that the central bank will leave this rate at 0.5 percent in the coming months. This overshadowed remarks about the potential for trade friction between the U.S. and Japan made earlier by an U.S. embassy official in Tokyo.
Lawrence Greenwood, the economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy said that the increases in Japan's current account could trigger trade tensions between the two countries.
"If (U.S. Trade Representative Charlene) Barshefsky or Clinton had said it is would have been taken much more seriously," said Ferridge at Commerzbank.
